summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a "vice against nature", and the same instrument made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment in employment and services.

A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. Article 23 of the Angolan Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression are located across Title II of the Constitution in the Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights.

No specific law allows transgender people in Angola to change the gender marker on official documents and passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that details entered into registration records should in general not be altered, while section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including name changes and changes where altered facts affect a person's legal identity and status, so a transgender person could in principle proceed under that section.

Angola recognises no same-sex couples. Social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant, and in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as "shameless" and "abominable" in national news magazines.

No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded in the sources. People living with HIV/AIDS are entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination.

Angolan organisations submitted a shadow report on the country's compliance with the regional human-rights charter for the 81st session of the commission, held in October and November 2024 in Banjul, documenting human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. Signatories included Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina, with support from ILGA and Synergia. Ahead of the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights' 74th session review of Angola, Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations filed a submission raising discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.
tangentialFactors:
A continental overview published on 28 October 2019 places Angola at the front of the African reforms it surveys, both for deleting the colonial-era offence and for criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services, and compares legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

Visible trans presence predates decriminalisation. A BBC profile of 12 April 2012 described the kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, as a mainstream star at 25 in a country the article characterised as Catholic, where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour.

In 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive the openly gay Israeli ambassador Isi Yanouka, allegedly because of his sexual orientation. The refusal was a diplomatic reception decision and not a visa rule.

The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms, although the government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.
localsOnly:
Two LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one, Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018. It had about 200 members at that time, is based in Luanda and maintains offices in Benguela and Lubango.

Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded. The first association, Acção Humana, launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programmes specifically for LGBT people have struggled to obtain NGO support. Some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education.

An HIV/AIDS educational programme for LGBT people is only beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International. A 2007 study estimated that roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men.
outOfScopeNotes:
No entry or visa provisions are recorded for Angola in the sources. The only entry-adjacent items are external reference links to asylumlaw.org packets on sexual minorities and HIV status used for asylum purposes, and to UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice on local laws and customs.

The sources do not record whether the Civil Registrar has in fact granted a gender-marker change under section 87 of the Código do Registo Civil. The availability of that route is a reading of the statutory text, and its application in practice is unresolved and not sourced.

No prosecution or enforcement case under the sexual-orientation discrimination offence is recorded in the inventory. Enforcement of the 2019 provision is therefore not sourced, and the absence of recorded cases is not evidence about filing practice.

The absence of shelters, safe houses and gender-neutral facilities is an absence in the sources rather than a verified inventory of what exists on the ground. No youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education are recorded.
